title: The notebook grew a UI. The contract still lives underneath.

## The question

A familiar promise in analytics says every new interface removes technical work. In practice, it often only moves the work. A friendlier screen can make a task easier to start while leaving ownership, definitions, and repeatability exactly where they were.

[Tools With Interactive UIs In Fabric Notebooks With Semantic Link Labs](https://blog.crossjoin.co.uk/2026/08/23/tools-with-interactive-uis-in-fabric-notebooks-with-semantic-link-labs/) gave me a useful version of that tension. Chris Webb shows Semantic Link Labs opening interactive tools inside a Fabric notebook: a lineage view that can inspect connected reports and broken visuals, plus a VertiPaq Analyzer, all reached with a small amount of code. If the notebook now has buttons and diagrams, what actually changes in how I build analytics, and what must stay boring underneath?

## The surface moved closer to the evidence

Most BI troubleshooting starts with a gap between where the problem is visible and where it can be investigated. Someone spots a broken visual in a report. Another person opens a workspace, traces a model, looks for a dependency, and eventually lands in code. Each handoff loses context.

Putting an interactive lineage tool inside the notebook compresses that distance. The workspace and semantic model can be selected where the investigation is already happening. The visual result sits beside the cells that opened it. That matters because exploration is rarely clean enough to justify writing a polished script before I know which question is worth keeping.

I do not read this as no-code replacing code. I read it as the interface becoming an on-ramp to a traceable workspace. The decision rule I would keep is simple: use the interface to shorten the path to evidence; use the notebook to preserve how you got there.

That is a better bargain than pretending every analyst should remember a library's full API before checking a lineage problem. It also beats a separate admin screen when the finding needs immediate investigation. The UI earns its place by reducing search cost, not by making the system less technical.

## A button is not the contract

Moving the surface does not settle the meaning below it. A lineage view can show that a report is connected to a semantic model. It cannot decide whether that connection is intended, who owns the measure, or whether two teams mean the same thing by revenue. A broken-visual check can find a symptom. It cannot tell me which release introduced it or whether the report is still part of a live decision process.

The same limit applies to VertiPaq analysis. A convenient view can expose model shape and invite the right performance questions. It does not choose the grain, define the KPI, or explain why a slow measure is allowed to remain because changing it would break a board pack.

This is where moving stacks create false confidence. The newest surface feels like the new architecture, so teams start storing judgment in clicks. Six months later the package, pane, or preferred workflow changes, and the only durable artifact is a screenshot in a chat thread. I want the opposite: changing tools around stable definitions, named ownership, and rerunnable checks.

## The review loop I would trust

I would start interactively. Open the notebook, select the model, use the lineage view to find the suspicious connection, and inspect the report in context. That is the fast path, and forcing a command-line ritual onto every first look would waste the capability the source is showing.

Once a finding becomes recurring, I would move the question into explicit cells and outputs. The notebook should say which workspace and model were inspected, what condition counts as a failure, and what was found. If the check has to run unattended, I would take it out of the click path entirely. A scheduled regression should not wait for someone to open an interactive widget.

The manual step stays where interpretation begins. Someone still decides whether a dependency is wrong, whether a model change is safe, and whether the evidence is strong enough to block a release. I am comfortable automating discovery before I automate that call.

Orbit uses the same split in a smaller system. Signals and project state can produce a weekly draft, but Slack Approve remains the publication gate. The interface makes review easier; it does not inherit the authority to publish. That boundary is more important than whether the reviewer arrived through code, a web page, or a button.

## Where convenience becomes debt

An interactive notebook UI is the wrong endpoint when the same question must pass every night, when reviewers need a stable diff, or when the result depends on notebook state that nobody else can reconstruct. It can also hide access problems: a tool may look self-contained while the person rerunning it lacks the workspace permissions or context of the original author.

The counter-case matters too. Requiring code for every inspection creates its own debt. It narrows who can test a suspicion and encourages people to export data into less governed tools. A UI beside the code can widen participation without separating the analysis from its technical context.

So I would not choose between interactive and reproducible as identities. I would choose based on the life of the question. Exploration can begin with controls. A repeated check graduates to code. A production gate needs an owner and an unattended test. The mistake is letting one surface pretend to serve all three.

## Takeaway

When the reporting stack moves, I do not need every interface to stay familiar. I need the path from evidence to decision to remain legible. Interactive tools inside Fabric notebooks look valuable because they bring inspection closer to the model and lower the cost of a first look.

But the UI is a handle, not the contract. I will use it to find the problem faster, then preserve the question, the check, and the owner in forms that can survive the next pane. If a result matters twice, it should not depend on remembering where I clicked the first time.
